subject: Pakistan Affairs
question_text: What was the Lahore Resolution of 1940 and why is it significant?
reference_answer: The Lahore Resolution was adopted at the All-India Muslim League session in Lahore in March 1940 (Jinnah presiding; moved by A. K. Fazlul Huq). It demanded that the areas where Muslims were numerically in a majority, in the north-western and eastern zones of India, be grouped to constitute independent states. It is widely regarded as the formal political basis of the demand for Pakistan.
evaluation_criteria: States the date, venue and party (March 1940, Lahore, All-India Muslim League)
Explains the core demand (grouping of Muslim-majority zones into independent states)
Links the resolution to the later Pakistan movement
candidate_answer: The Lahore Resolution was passed by the All-India Muslim League in March 1940 at its Lahore session, presided over by Jinnah and moved by A. K. Fazlul Huq. It called for the Muslim-majority regions in the north-west and east of British India to be grouped into independent states, with full autonomy and sovereignty for each unit. It is treated as the founding political document of the demand for a separate Muslim homeland, later shortened in common usage to the 'Pakistan Resolution', and it shaped the Muslim League's strategy for the rest of the freedom movement.
rag_relevance_rationale: No dedicated 'Pakistan Movement'/1940s freedom-movement source in the indexed corpus beyond brief syllabus topic headings.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
question_text: Describe the main features of the Objectives Resolution of 1949 and its role in Pakistan's constitutional development.
reference_answer: Passed by the first Constituent Assembly in March 1949 (moved by Liaquat Ali Khan), it declared that sovereignty over the universe belongs to Allah and that authority is exercised by the people as a sacred trust through their chosen representatives. It promised democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance and social justice as enunciated by Islam, protection of minorities, fundamental rights and an independent judiciary. It served as a preamble to later constitutions and was made a substantive part of the Constitution as Article 2A in 1985.
evaluation_criteria: Gives the date and mover of the resolution
Lists its main principles (sovereignty of Allah, democracy, rights, minorities, judiciary)
Explains its later constitutional status (preamble; Article 2A)
candidate_answer: The Objectives Resolution was passed in 1973 by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's government as the preamble to the new Constitution, and it declared Pakistan a secular state where religion would play no role in governance. It was never made a substantive part of the Constitution and has no legal effect today.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
question_text: Critically analyse the causes that led to the separation of East Pakistan in 1971.
reference_answer: Historians point to several interacting causes: perceived economic disparity and exploitation of the eastern wing; the language question (1948 and 1952) and wider cultural grievances; political marginalisation and long delays in constitution-making; dominance of the civil-military establishment; geographic separation of the two wings; the failure to transfer power after the 1970 elections in which the Awami League won a majority; the military action of March 1971; and Indian military intervention in December 1971. The Hamoodur Rahman Commission examined the events. A strong answer weighs these factors rather than listing them.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies political, economic, cultural and military causes
Weighs the relative importance of causes instead of only listing them
Refers to specific events (1952, 1970 elections, March and December 1971)
Maintains a balanced, evidence-based tone
candidate_answer: East Pakistan separated in 1971 mainly because of language problems after Urdu was imposed and because the army took action in March 1971. India also got involved and helped East Pakistan become Bangladesh. There were also some economic issues between the two wings.

subject: Pakistan Affairs
question_text: Evaluate the role of the judiciary, including the doctrine of necessity, in Pakistan's political history.
reference_answer: In Federation of Pakistan v. Maulvi Tamizuddin Khan (1955) the Federal Court validated the Governor-General's dissolution of the Constituent Assembly, and in State v. Dosso (1958) it used the doctrine of necessity and Kelsen's idea of a 'grundnorm' to validate the first martial law. Asma Jilani v. Government of the Punjab (1972) overruled Dosso, but Begum Nusrat Bhutto v. Chief of Army Staff (1977) again validated a coup on grounds of necessity, as did the Zafar Ali Shah case (2000). Critics say these rulings weakened constitutionalism; supporters note later assertions of judicial independence.
evaluation_criteria: Names and explains at least three landmark cases
Explains the doctrine of necessity
Evaluates the long-term effect on constitutionalism
Notes both validation and corrective judgments
candidate_answer: Pakistan's judiciary has always sided with whoever is in power, and the doctrine of necessity was basically invented so judges could keep their jobs under military rule. Every single martial law in Pakistan's history was approved by the courts without exception, and this proves the judiciary has never had any real independence.
rag_relevance_rationale: Specific case-law/legal-history topic; the RAG corpus (Constitution text, syllabus outlines) does not contain case names like Dosso/Asma Jilani, so there is nothing to corroborate or contradict this sweeping claim.

subject: Current Affairs
question_text: Discuss the role of the IMF in Pakistan's economic management and the debates surrounding it.
reference_answer: Pakistan has repeatedly entered IMF programmes to address balance-of-payments pressures. Programmes usually carry conditionality such as fiscal consolidation, higher tax revenue, energy-subsidy reform and a more flexible exchange rate. Supporters argue they restore macroeconomic stability and confidence; critics point to inflation, social costs, limits on policy autonomy and the recurring need for new programmes, which reflects structural weaknesses such as a low tax-to-GDP ratio, weak exports and energy-sector circular debt.

Describes typical conditions
Presents both supportive and critical views
Identifies underlying structural causes

subject: Current Affairs
question_text: Assess the Paris Agreement and the idea of climate justice for developing countries.
reference_answer: The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius and pursue 1.5 degrees, with countries submitting nationally determined contributions. Climate justice argues that countries that contributed least to emissions suffer most and need finance, technology and adaptation support under the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Agreement on a loss-and-damage fund at COP27 (2022) was a step in this direction, but gaps in climate finance and ambition remain, which matters for highly exposed states like Pakistan.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the main goals and mechanisms of the Paris Agreement
Explains climate justice and differentiated responsibility
Applies the issue to developing countries such as Pakistan
Evaluates progress and gaps
candidate_answer: Rather than framing this mainly as a moral obligation on rich countries, I'd argue the stronger case for climate finance to developing countries like Pakistan is self-interested: unmitigated climate damage in the Global South (mass displacement, food-security shocks, pandemics) imposes direct economic and security costs on wealthy nations too, so climate finance is best sold domestically in donor countries as risk management, not charity -- while the Paris Agreement's 1.5C target and NDC architecture remain the right technical framework regardless of which argument persuades funders.
rag_relevance_rationale: Economic Survey's dedicated Climate Change chapter is well-indexed and topically well-aligned with this question.

subject: Current Affairs
question_text: What is the circular debt in Pakistan's power sector and how can it be addressed?
reference_answer: Circular debt is the accumulation of unpaid bills along the energy supply chain: consumers and distribution companies do not pay fully, so power producers and fuel suppliers go unpaid, and the government often covers the gap through subsidies and borrowing. Causes include transmission and distribution losses, electricity theft, under-recovery of tariffs, high capacity payments and delayed subsidy payments. Solutions include tariff rationalisation, reducing losses and theft, better governance and privatisation or restructuring of distribution companies, renegotiating costly contracts and expanding cheaper generation.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the mechanism of circular debt
Identifies several causes
Proposes concrete reforms
candidate_answer: This refers to the chain of unrecovered receivables that builds up across Pakistan's electricity supply chain: when end-users and the distribution utilities don't fully settle their bills, the shortfall cascades upstream to generation companies and fuel suppliers, who in turn can't pay their own creditors, and the state ends up plugging the gap with subsidies and debt. Root causes include transmission losses, non-payment/theft, under-pricing relative to the true cost of supply, and fixed capacity charges owed regardless of actual offtake. Fixes center on right-sizing tariffs, cutting losses and theft, and restructuring or privatising the distribution companies.
rag_relevance_rationale: Economic Survey covers energy/fiscal themes generally but 'circular debt' specifically is a narrow technical term not confirmed as a strong independent match in prior retrieval tests.

subject: Current Affairs
question_text: What is the World Trade Organization (WTO) and why does it matter for developing countries?
reference_answer: The WTO, established in 1995 as the successor to the GATT, sets rules for international trade, provides a forum for trade negotiations and operates a dispute-settlement system. Pakistan has been a member since its creation in 1995. For developing countries it offers rules-based market access and protection against arbitrary trade measures, but critics argue that its rules and negotiating power favour wealthier economies and that agriculture and intellectual property rules can disadvantage poorer states.

candidate_answer: The World Trade Organization was established in 1995 as the successor to the GATT. It sets the rules governing international trade between its member states, provides a standing forum for trade negotiations, and runs a binding dispute-settlement mechanism so members can challenge each other's trade measures rather than resorting to unilateral retaliation. Pakistan has been a member since the WTO's founding in 1995. For developing countries the WTO offers predictable, rules-based access to export markets and protection against arbitrary tariffs or quotas, but critics argue the rules on agriculture and intellectual property were negotiated on terms that favour wealthier, more industrialised members.

subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
question_text: What is the separation of powers and how is it reflected in Pakistan's Constitution?
reference_answer: Separation of powers divides state authority among the legislature, the executive and the judiciary so that each acts as a check on the others. In Pakistan's 1973 Constitution the legislature is Parliament (the National Assembly and the Senate), the executive is the President, the Prime Minister and the Cabinet in a parliamentary system, and the judiciary is headed by the Supreme Court. In practice the boundaries and balance have been contested over time.
evaluation_criteria: Defines separation of powers and checks and balances
Maps the three organs to Pakistan's institutions
Acknowledges practical tensions
candidate_answer: Separation of powers means the government is split into different branches so no one part has too much control. Pakistan has a parliament, a prime minister, and courts. This is supposed to stop any one branch from becoming too powerful, although in practice the military has also played a big role.

subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
question_text: Describe the main features of the Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan.
reference_answer: Passed in April 2010, it removed the President's power to dissolve the National Assembly, abolished the Concurrent Legislative List and devolved subjects to the provinces, renamed the North-West Frontier Province as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, strengthened the Council of Common Interests, and inserted rights such as the right to education (Article 25A) and the right to information (Article 19A). It also changed the procedure for judicial appointments through a Judicial Commission and a parliamentary committee.
evaluation_criteria: Gives the year and main purpose
Lists at least four specific changes
Explains the effect on federalism
candidate_answer: The Eighteenth Amendment, passed in April 2010, was the most significant rebalancing of Pakistan's federation since 1973. It stripped the President of the power to unilaterally dissolve the National Assembly, restoring the Constitution to a genuinely parliamentary form. It abolished the Concurrent Legislative List entirely, devolving subjects like education, health and agriculture to the provinces, and strengthened the Council of Common Interests as the forum for resolving federal-provincial disputes over the newly devolved areas. The North-West Frontier Province was renamed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It also inserted new fundamental rights -- the right to education under Article 25A and the right to information under Article 19A -- and reformed the judicial-appointments process by creating a Judicial Commission alongside a parliamentary committee.

subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
question_text: What are Fundamental Rights under the 1973 Constitution? Name and explain at least five.
reference_answer: Fundamental Rights are in Part II, Chapter 1 of the Constitution (Articles 8-28), and laws inconsistent with them are void (Article 8). They include security of person (Article 9), safeguards on arrest and detention (Article 10), the right to a fair trial (Article 10A), inviolability of dignity (Article 14), freedom of movement (Article 15), freedom of association (Article 17), freedom of speech (Article 19), the right to information (Article 19A), freedom of religion (Article 20), the right to property (Article 23), equality of citizens (Article 25) and the right to education (Article 25A).
evaluation_criteria: Locates fundamental rights in the Constitution
Names at least five with article numbers
Notes that laws inconsistent with them are void
candidate_answer: Fundamental Rights in Pakistan's Constitution are found in Part I and are only advisory -- the government can override them whenever it decides national security requires it, since Article 8 says Parliament may pass any law regardless of the rights chapter. Examples include the right to free healthcare (Article 9), the right to a government job (Article 15), and the right to foreign travel without a passport (Article 19).
rag_relevance_rationale: Constitution PDF's Part II Fundamental Rights chapter (actual articles 8-28) is extensively indexed and directly contradicts every specific claim in this answer (wrong Part, wrong effect of Article 8, three invented rights).

subject: Governance and Constitutional Studies
question_text: Evaluate the accountability institutions in Pakistan such as the National Accountability Bureau, the Auditor-General and the Ombudsman.
reference_answer: The Auditor-General of Pakistan (Articles 168-171) audits federal and provincial accounts and reports to the legislature, supporting parliamentary oversight. The Wafaqi Mohtasib (Federal Ombudsman, established 1983) investigates complaints of maladministration by federal agencies. The National Accountability Bureau, created by the 1999 ordinance, investigates and prosecutes corruption. Strengths include a legal mandate and public access; weaknesses include allegations of political bias, weak follow-up on audit findings, overlapping institutions and limited prosecutorial success. Reforms focus on independence, transparency and parliamentary follow-up.

Evaluates strengths and weaknesses
Proposes reforms
candidate_answer: None of Pakistan's accountability bodies actually work. NAB is completely captured by whoever is in government at the time and has never once successfully prosecuted a case fairly, the Auditor-General's reports are always ignored and never even read by Parliament, and the Ombudsman's office doesn't really do anything beyond paperwork.

subject: International Relations
question_text: What is the role of the United Nations Security Council?
reference_answer: The Security Council bears primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. It has 15 members: five permanent members with veto power (the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia and China) and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. Under Chapter VII of the UN Charter it can adopt binding decisions, impose sanctions and authorise peacekeeping or the use of force.

candidate_answer: The UN Security Council carries the primary responsibility, under the UN Charter, for maintaining international peace and security. It has fifteen members: five permanent members -- the US, UK, France, Russia and China -- each holding veto power, and ten non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, it can make legally binding decisions, impose economic sanctions, and authorise peacekeeping missions or, in the last resort, the use of force.

subject: International Relations
question_text: Explain the theory of realism in international relations.
reference_answer: Realism holds that states are the main actors in an anarchic international system with no central authority, that they pursue power and national interest, and that security is achieved through self-help and balance of power. Classical realists such as Morgenthau ground this in human nature; structural realists (neorealists) such as Waltz stress the structure of the system. Related ideas include the security dilemma. Critics argue it underestimates cooperation, institutions and non-state actors.
evaluation_criteria: States realism's core assumptions
Distinguishes classical and structural realism
Offers at least one critique
candidate_answer: Realism says that in international relations, countries mainly care about power and survival because there's no higher authority above states. Morgenthau is a famous realist. It doesn't talk much about cooperation between countries.

subject: International Relations
question_text: Discuss the Kashmir dispute in the context of international law and bilateral agreements between India and Pakistan.
reference_answer: The status of Jammu and Kashmir has been addressed in UN Security Council resolutions calling for a plebiscite and in bilateral agreements. The Tashkent Declaration (1966) and the Simla Agreement (1972), which converted the ceasefire line into the Line of Control and committed the parties to settle differences bilaterally, and the Lahore Declaration (1999) are key texts. Pakistan stresses the UN resolutions and the right of self-determination; India stresses bilateralism and treats Kashmir as an internal matter, a position sharpened by its August 2019 revocation of Article 370. An analysis should present both positions neutrally and consider paths such as dialogue and confidence-building.
evaluation_criteria: Covers the UN dimension and the bilateral agreements
Presents both countries' positions accurately
Maintains neutrality and analytical tone
Considers the way forward
candidate_answer: Rather than treating this as simply 'who is right,' I think the more useful CSS-exam framing is that both the UN-resolution track (plebiscite, self-determination) and the bilateral track (Simla, Lahore) have been allowed to coexist unresolved for over seven decades precisely because neither side has had an incentive to formally abandon its preferred legal framework, and any realistic way forward probably has to accept that ambiguity rather than resolve it -- confidence-building measures and trade/people-to-people contact across the Line of Control are more achievable in the near term than a final legal settlement.

subject: International Relations
question_text: What are the main sources of international law?
reference_answer: According to Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice, the main sources are international conventions (treaties), international custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law, and the general principles of law recognised by civilised nations. Judicial decisions and the teachings of highly qualified publicists are subsidiary means for determining rules of law.

Refers to Article 38 of the ICJ Statute
Identifies subsidiary sources
candidate_answer: Per Article 38 of the International Court of Justice's founding statute, international law is primarily drawn from treaties between states, from customary practice that states follow out of a sense of legal obligation, and from general legal principles shared across domestic legal systems. Where these leave a gap, the Court may also look to prior case law and to the writings of leading legal scholars as secondary, persuasive-only material.

subject: English
question_text: Explain the essential qualities of a good precis.
reference_answer: A good precis reduces the passage to roughly one-third of its length while keeping the main idea and essential points. It is written in the candidate's own words, in the third person and in indirect speech, avoids quotations, examples and personal opinion, is coherent and continuous in a single paragraph, and carries a suitable title.

candidate_answer: A good precis compresses a passage to roughly a third of its original length while preserving its central idea and essential supporting points. It must be written entirely in the candidate's own words rather than lifted phrases, in the third person and in reported (indirect) speech even if the original used direct speech, as a single continuous and coherent paragraph. Direct quotation, illustrative examples and the writer's personal opinion should all be omitted, and the precis should be given a short, accurate title.

subject: English
question_text: Explain denotation and connotation and why they matter in persuasive writing.
reference_answer: Denotation is the literal dictionary meaning of a word; connotation is the emotional or cultural association it carries. 'Thrifty' and 'stingy' share a denotation but differ in connotation. In persuasive writing, careful diction shapes tone and influences the reader, so writers choose words whose connotations support their argument while avoiding loaded language that undermines credibility.

subject: English
question_text: Explain ethos, pathos and logos and how they are used in argument.
reference_answer: Rhetorical appeals described by Aristotle are ethos (credibility and character of the speaker), pathos (appeal to the audience's emotions) and logos (appeal to logic, evidence and reasoning). Effective argument usually combines them: logos provides sound evidence and structure, ethos builds trust through expertise and fairness, and pathos engages the audience, with the caution that emotional appeals should not replace evidence.

subject: General Knowledge
question_text: Explain the water scarcity challenge in Pakistan and the debate over dams and water management.
reference_answer: Per-capita water availability has declined sharply with population growth, and Pakistan's storage capacity is small relative to river flows. Tarbela and Mangla are the major reservoirs. Debates include new storage such as Diamer-Bhasha, the long-contested Kalabagh project and inter-provincial water sharing concerns, inefficient irrigation, groundwater depletion and climate-driven variability. Solutions discussed include additional storage, efficient irrigation and pricing, aquifer recharge, and cooperation under the Indus Waters Treaty framework.

subject: General Knowledge
question_text: Differentiate between the IMF and the World Bank.
reference_answer: Both were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference. The International Monetary Fund promotes international monetary cooperation and financial stability and provides short- to medium-term financing to countries with balance-of-payments problems, usually with policy conditions. The World Bank group provides long-term loans, grants and technical assistance for development projects and poverty reduction, such as infrastructure, health and education.

Distinguishes the mandate of each institution

candidate_answer: Both institutions trace back to the 1944 Bretton Woods conference, but they serve different purposes. The Fund's mandate is macroeconomic and monetary stability: it extends relatively short- to medium-term, conditionality-attached financing to member states facing balance-of-payments crises, acting essentially as a lender of last resort to sovereigns. The Bank Group's mandate is long-horizon development: it funds infrastructure, health, education and poverty-reduction projects through long-term loans, concessional credit and grants, aimed at raising living standards rather than stabilising a currency crisis.

subject: Islamic Studies
question_text: Explain the sources of Islamic law (Shariah).
reference_answer: The primary sources are the Quran and the Sunnah (the sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet, peace be upon him). The secondary or derived sources commonly accepted are Ijma (consensus of qualified scholars) and Qiyas (analogical reasoning). Other principles such as Istihsan, Maslaha and Urf are used with varying acceptance among schools of jurisprudence, and Ijtihad is the process of reasoning that applies them to new questions.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes primary from secondary sources
Explains Ijma and Qiyas
Mentions Ijtihad and differences among schools
candidate_answer: The primary sources of Islamic law are the Quran, as the literal revealed word of God, and the Sunnah, the recorded sayings, actions and tacit approvals of the Prophet (peace be upon him), which explains and supplements the Quran. Where these are silent on a specific question, jurists turn to secondary sources: Ijma, the consensus of qualified scholars on a ruling, and Qiyas, analogical reasoning that extends an established ruling to a new but similar case. Depending on the school of jurisprudence, additional tools such as Istihsan (juristic preference for the more equitable outcome), Maslaha (consideration of public welfare) and local Urf (custom) are also drawn upon, with Ijtihad being the overarching intellectual effort of applying all of these to a new question.
rag_relevance_rationale: Both the Islamic Studies syllabus section and the Constitution's Islamic Provisions (Part IX) are indexed; prior evaluations show moderate-to-strong retrieval (~0.4+ P@5) for closely related queries.

subject: Islamic Studies
question_text: Discuss the concept of Ijtihad and its relevance in addressing contemporary challenges.
reference_answer: Ijtihad is independent reasoning by a qualified jurist (mujtahid) to derive rulings where the sources give no explicit text. It was central in the formative period of jurisprudence; there is debate over whether its 'gate' was ever closed. Allama Iqbal described ijtihad as the principle of movement in Islam and proposed that it be exercised collectively through a legislative assembly. Contemporary areas include banking and finance, biomedical ethics, technology and the rights and duties of citizens in modern states. A good answer notes the required qualifications and limits of ijtihad.

candidate_answer: Ijtihad is the exercise of independent juristic effort by a qualified scholar to work out a ruling on a matter the primary texts don't address explicitly. There's long-running debate over whether this avenue was effectively shut after the formative centuries of Islamic law or always remained open to a sufficiently qualified scholar. Iqbal reframed it as what he called the 'principle of movement' within Islam, arguing it should be exercised collectively by an elected legislative body rather than left to individual jurists alone. subject: Islamic Studies
question_text: Evaluate the concept of jihad in Islam and distinguish it from terrorism.
reference_answer: Jihad literally means striving or struggle and covers moral and spiritual self-discipline, the pursuit of knowledge and justice, and, under strict conditions, armed defence. Classical rules require legitimate authority, a just cause and restraint: non-combatants, women, children and places of worship must not be harmed, and the Quran stresses that taking one innocent life is like killing all humanity. Terrorism, which targets civilians to spread fear for political ends, violates these principles; in Pakistan a national narrative document of religious scholars, Paigham-e-Pakistan (2018), rejected such violence in the name of religion.

Civilian casualties are an unfortunate but accepted part of this obligation.

subject: Political Science
question_text: Explain the theory of separation of powers in classical political thought, referencing Montesquieu.
reference_answer: Montesquieu, in 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748), argued that liberty is best secured by dividing state power among a legislature, an executive and a judiciary, each held by different hands, so that no single branch can exercise all of government and each can check the others' overreach. He drew on (and arguably idealised) the English constitutional model of his time. The idea strongly influenced later constitutional design, including the US Constitution's checks-and-balances structure.
evaluation_criteria: Names Montesquieu and the source text
Explains the three-branch division and its purpose
Notes its influence on later constitutions
candidate_answer: In 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748), Montesquieu argued that political liberty is only secure when the power of government is divided among three distinct branches -- a legislature to make laws, an executive to enforce them, and a judiciary to interpret and apply them -- held by different persons or bodies, so that each branch can check the excesses of the others. He developed this partly from an admiring (and somewhat idealised) reading of the English constitution of his era. The idea became foundational to modern constitutional design, most explicitly in the US Constitution's system of checks and balances, and remains the standard reference point for separation-of-powers doctrine worldwide.

question_text: Explain the basic structure of the solar system and the Earth's place in it.
reference_answer: The solar system consists of the Sun at its centre, eight planets orbiting it (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, and smaller bodies such as asteroids, comets and dwarf planets. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, the only one known to support life, orbiting at a distance (about 150 million km, one astronomical unit) that keeps it in the Sun's habitable zone where liquid water can exist.

candidate_answer: Our solar system is centred on the Sun, which holds roughly 99.8% of the system's total mass and whose gravity keeps everything else in orbit. Orbiting it, in order of increasing distance, are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, along with their moons, plus asteroids, comets and dwarf planets such as Pluto. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, at a distance of about 150 million kilometres (defined as one astronomical unit), which places it within the Sun's 'habitable zone' -- the narrow range of orbital distances where temperatures allow water to exist as a liquid, which is why Earth, uniquely among the planets we know of, supports life.

subject: General Science and Ability
question_text: What is the greenhouse effect and how does it contribute to climate change?
reference_answer: The greenhouse effect is the natural process by which gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour trap some of the Sun's heat in the atmosphere, keeping Earth warm enough to support life. Human activity, especially burning fossil fuels and deforestation, has sharply increased concentrations of these greenhouse gases, intensifying the effect beyond its natural balance and driving global warming and climate change, including rising sea levels, more extreme weather and shifting precipitation patterns.
